lead: System control changes the application itself, not a scene object. It loads a scene, saves work, changes a mode, opens help or quits. Menus, voice commands, gesture commands and mixtures of these carry such commands. The idea exists because a user must run the whole XR application, not only move a virtual cube. You meet it in a VR training app that switches lessons, in an AR repair guide that jumps to the next step, and in a headset home screen that changes settings. Some syllabi call this command and control.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for selection and object manipulation, and Unit 2 for input devices and gesture hardware.

blocks.text: System control is a command that changes the application state. Examples are load scene, save work, change a setting, open help, undo and quit. It does not change a scene object. Chapter 5.1 covers object selection and manipulation. Chapter 5.2 covers travel. The same hardware can do both jobs. In an AR repair guide, pinching a virtual bolt turns the model: scene control. Saying “next step” changes the lesson: system control. The meaning of the command decides the class, not the device. Classify system control by channel: graphical menus, voice, gesture and multimodal. A small command set may use one channel. A large set needs menus or a mix. A command may open a menu, and the menu item is a second command. Keep system commands few and named clearly. Some syllabi call this command and control.

Graphical menus show commands as visible choices. A 2D menu sits on a flat panel in the headset or on a controller screen. It is stable, legible and familiar; use it for settings. A 3D menu places choices in space around the user or on a virtual object. It uses depth and spatial memory, but watch occlusion, reach and text size. A pie menu puts items around a circle. The user points or flicks toward a sector; the chosen sector highlights. Pie menus are fast for small sets. A marking menu is a pie menu that can hide labels after the user learns stroke directions. A novice presses and sees the pie; an expert draws the mark directly. Steps for a pie menu: open with a button or gesture; aim at a sector; release to choose. Give feedback on the highlighted item before release.

Voice commands use a grammar: a list of allowed words and patterns, such as “open scene” or “set mode”. Keep phrases short and distinct. Use push-to-talk or a wake word to avoid false activation. Ask for confirmation before destructive commands: “delete all, yes or no”. For error recovery, show the recognised text, repeat the prompt, offer alternatives and allow undo. Speech recognition returns a confidence score; a low score should trigger a retry. Gesture commands are either pose or motion. A pose is a static hand shape, such as a thumbs-up. A motion is a path over time, such as a swipe. Delimiting marks the start and end: a dwell, a pinch, a button press or a fixed start pose. Without delimiting, normal hand movement triggers commands. Choose gestures that are distinct from object manipulation gestures. Tools include menu toolkits, speech SDKs and gesture recognisers.

Multimodal system control uses more than one channel. Fusion combines the evidence into one command. Complementary input: voice says “move this” while the hand points to the target. Redundant input: say “confirm” and press a button. Late fusion combines channel decisions inside a short time window. If channels disagree, use a priority rule or ask the user; show the fused command before it runs. Weight by command counts; do not average rates across unequal counts. Design rules: show the current mode; give visual and audio feedback; make commands discoverable with help and hints; stop false activation with thresholds, confirmation and undo.
S = Σ c_i s_i, r = S / Σ c_i
blocks.where: c_i is the number of commands on channel i; s_i is that channel’s success rate; S is the total number of successful commands; r is the overall success rate.

figure.caption: Each channel's successes are its command count times its own rate: 63 of 70 voice, 16 of 20 gesture, 10 of 10 menu. Together that is 89 of 100, so the app succeeds 89% of the time, not the plain average of 90%.

examples.question: An app accepts voice and gesture. In 100 commands, 70 are voice, 20 gesture and 10 menu. Voice succeeds 90% of its commands, gesture 80%, menu 100%. Compute total successful commands and overall success rate.
examples.answer: The app completes 89 successful commands, so the overall success rate is 89%.
examples.check:
voice_cmds = 70
gesture_cmds = 20
menu_cmds = 10
voice_succ = voice_cmds * 0.90
gesture_succ = gesture_cmds * 0.80
menu_succ = menu_cmds * 1.00
total = voice_succ + gesture_succ + menu_succ
rate = total / (voice_cmds + gesture_cmds + menu_cmds) * 100
print(voice_succ)
print(gesture_succ)
print(menu_succ)
print(total)
print(rate)

traps: Do not average success percentages across unequal command counts. Weight by the number of commands on each channel, as in 70 voice, 20 gesture and 10 menu commands.

System control changes the application; object manipulation changes a scene object. Rotating a virtual bolt is scene control, while saying “next step” is system control, even if both use a hand gesture.
A pie menu shows items around a circle. A marking menu uses a remembered stroke direction and may hide labels. They are related but not the same exam answer.
Voice grammar is not the speech recogniser itself. The grammar limits allowed phrases; the recogniser maps audio to words and returns confidence.
Pose and motion gestures differ: a pose is a static hand shape, while a motion is a path over time. Delimiting is needed for both to avoid false activation.

quiz.q: Define system control and give three example commands.
quiz.a: System control changes the application state, not a scene object. Examples: load scene, save work, open help, change settings, undo, quit.

quiz.q: Why is confirmation used for voice commands?
quiz.a: Speech recognition can mishear, so a destructive or costly command should be checked. The app asks a yes/no question, shows the recognised phrase and allows undo.

quiz.q: Distinguish a pose gesture from a motion gesture, with one example each.
quiz.a: A pose is a static hand shape, such as a thumbs-up. A motion is a path over time, such as a swipe. Both need delimiting to mark start and end.

quiz.q: In 50 commands, 30 are voice at 90% success, 15 are gesture at 80% success and 5 are menu at 100% success. Compute total successes and overall success rate.
A VR app has many false activations from the gesture “open menu” while the user points. Propose two design changes and explain each.
quiz.a: Require a clear start pose or dwell so pointing does not trigger the command. Move “open menu” to a button or voice command. Add a threshold and show feedback before running. Provide undo for any remaining false activations.

quiz.q: What is multimodal fusion in system control?
quiz.a: Multimodal fusion combines evidence from more than one channel, such as voice and gesture, into one system command.

quiz.q: Why are pie menus fast for a small command set?
quiz.a: Items sit around a circle, so the user flicks in a direction instead of travelling to a list. Direction and spatial memory reduce search time. Marking menus extend this by letting experts draw the mark without looking.

quiz.q: Compare a 2D menu and a 3D menu for headset settings.
quiz.a: A 2D menu is stable, legible and familiar, so it suits settings and text-heavy lists. A 3D menu uses spatial memory and can place choices in the world, but it risks occlusion, reach problems and small text. For settings, 2D is usually safer; use 3D for spatial commands.

beyond: Not for the exam. XR operating systems now blend gaze, pinch and voice, so system control is becoming a small command language rather than a row of buttons. Hand-tracking toolkits expose pose and motion recognisers, and speech SDKs expose grammars and confidence scores. Research looks at error-aware fusion and adaptive menus that learn frequent commands. Search terms: command and control 3D interaction, multimodal fusion, marking menus, voice grammar, gesture delimiting.
